heard: Soviet orbital satellites once confirmed an incoming nuclear strike with highest reliability. On September 26, 1983, early warning screens alerted duty officer Stanislav Petrov to five American missiles. With nuclear detonation estimated 20 to 25 minutes away, the computer insisted an attack was underway. Yet Petrov suspected a real American strike would be an overwhelming barrage, not five isolated launches. Soviet ground-based radar installations showed clear skies beyond the horizon, confirming his suspicion. Petrov decided against reporting an attack, alerting headquarters instead that the system had malfunctioned. Later investigations revealed orbital satellites had encountered a rare alignment with the sun. Blinded by the glare, the satellite sensors mistook sunlight, reflecting off high-altitude clouds for missile launches. Glinting sunlight bouncing off clouds had triggered humanity's closest nuclear false alarm.
